summary: Help 7–9 year-olds name everyday types of energy — kinetic (movement), elastic (stretched or wound), gravitational/potential (raised), thermal (hot), light, sound, electrical and chemical — by anchoring each word to a concrete, observable example they can point to. The single most important move is to sort these words into 'STORED / waiting (or doing)' (chemical in a battery or food, elastic in a stretched or wound spring, gravitational energy in a raised object, thermal energy in a hot drink, movement/kinetic in a moving ball) versus 'ON THE MOVE / being transferred' (light, sound, heat flowing from hotter to cooler things, electric current), and to describe simple devices with 'energy is transferred / moves from here to there' rather than 'changes form'. This plants the stores-and-transfer distinction that later schooling builds on, without joules or quantification. Note: in England's national curriculum this age band has no formal primary energy topic (energy appears at KS3; other UK curricula such as Scotland's differ) and NGSS grade 4 gives qualitative definitions only, so this is vocabulary anchored to phenomena, not a formal 'list the forms of energy' expectation.
misconceptions: Thinking only living or moving things 'have energy', so a still spring, raised object or battery at rest has none — missing stored energy.
Treating light, sound and electric current as the same kind of 'stuff' as chemical or movement energy, rather than as energy on the move — the seed of the later store-vs-pathway error.
Reading 'energy transformation' as energy literally changing into a different substance.
Confusing energy with the object or fuel itself, or with force, 'power', or temperature (loose everyday usage).
Believing energy gets 'used up' and disappears (planted early by 'the battery ran out') — it is the fuel/battery that is used up, the energy is transferred elsewhere.

activities.title: Tap-and-name a busy familiar scene
steps: Look at a rich familiar scene (kitchen or playground) containing taggable energy sources: a ball flying, a battery in a remote, a torch shining, a drum sounding, a steaming kettle or hot drink, a stretched spring, a wind-up toy.

Point to each object and say its energy word, a one-line kid-friendly meaning, and a matching everyday example (moving ball = movement/kinetic; battery or food = chemical store; torch = light; drum = sound; hot drink or kettle = thermal; stretched spring = elastic; ball on a high shelf = raised/gravitational store).

For each object answer 'is this energy waiting, or on the move?' and then say the fuller sentence, e.g. 'The battery STORES chemical energy; when the torch is on, that energy is on the MOVE as light.'
Use the non-examples too: a still ball has no movement energy; a switched-off torch gives no light.
activities.insight: Each everyday energy word names something you can point to in a real scene, and a hidden meaning + example + non-example fences exactly what each word does and does not cover.

activities.title: Sort the scene: STORED / waiting vs ON THE MOVE
steps: Take every energy word from the scene and place it in one of two columns: 'STORED / waiting (or doing)' or 'ON THE MOVE / being transferred'.

Put chemical (battery, food), elastic (stretched or wound spring), a raised object (ball on a high shelf) and the thermal energy of a hot drink into STORED because the energy waits there even when nothing moves; put the moving ball's movement/kinetic energy there too, as energy an object has while it is doing something; put light, sound, heat flowing out from a hot thing to cooler surroundings, and electric current into ON THE MOVE.

After sorting the whole scene, say what pattern you notice — light, sound, heat flowing out of hot things and electric current tend to land in 'on the move', while chemical, elastic, gravitational, thermal (in a hot thing) and movement sit in 'stored or doing'.
Say two sentences for one device: a labelling sentence ('A moving ball has ___ energy') and a transfer sentence ('The battery stores chemical energy and transfers it to the torch as light').
activities.insight: Some energy is stored and waiting in things that can be completely still (including the thermal energy of a hot drink), movement is energy an object has while it is doing something, and light, sound, heat flowing from hotter to cooler things and electric current are energy on the move being transferred from one place to another — energy 'moves from here to there' rather than turning into a different substance.

activities.title: Watch the energy move through a device
steps: Watch or act out one device from start to end: wind up a toy and release it, or switch on a torch, keeping attention on where the energy starts and where it goes.

For the wind-up toy: say that winding stores elastic energy in the spring; releasing transfers that stored energy to the toy so it now has movement (kinetic) energy; all the while, rubbing in the gears and between the wheels and floor, and pushing through the air, transfers energy away to the surroundings as heat (and a little sound); once the spring has unwound, nothing keeps refilling the movement energy, so the toy slows and stops.
For the torch: say the battery stores chemical energy; when switched on, that energy is on the move along the wire and leaves the torch mostly as light, with some as heat (the bulb gets warm).
Mark out loud the 'store' and the 'on the move' moment for each device, keeping it qualitative with no numbers.
activities.insight: Dynamic words like 'transfer' and 'kinetic' name something you can watch happen: stored energy being transferred so an object starts moving, and energy travelling out of a device, so the words describe a process not just a label.

activities.title: Retrieval practice: match, sort and complete sentences
steps: Match each energy word to a picture of its everyday example.
Sort a fresh set of words into 'stored' versus 'being transferred'.
Complete sentences about familiar devices, e.g. 'A moving ball has ___ energy' and 'The battery stores ___ energy, and the torch gives out ___.'
For a torch and a toaster, name the energy that goes IN and the useful energy that comes OUT of each.
activities.insight: Secure recall of which word fits which example, and which column each word belongs to, consolidates the vocabulary after it has been built.

activities.title: Explain it back to an 'energy detective'
steps: Answer short spoken prompts about a scene or device, e.g. 'Point to where the energy is stored here', 'Is the torch's light stored or on the move?', 'Where was the car's energy a moment BEFORE you let it go?'
For a ball sitting still on a high shelf, say whether it has any energy stored, what type, and how you could release it.
Explain, in your own words, the energy story of a device, with the listener naming your idea back to you.
activities.insight: Saying where energy is stored and where it goes, out loud and in your own words, strengthens and checks the vocabulary beyond simply recognising it.

checkQuestion: Here's a wind-up toy car: you turn the key, let go, and it races across the floor, then slows and stops. Tell me the story of the toy using energy words — where the energy is stored to begin with, what type it becomes when the car races, and what happens to it as the car slows down.
checkAnswer: Winding the key stores elastic (potential) energy in the spring. When released, that stored energy is transferred and becomes kinetic energy — the energy of motion — as the car races. As the car rubs on the floor the energy is transferred away as heat (and a little sound) to the surroundings, so it slows and stops. The story uses 'stored' and 'transfer/transform' and names elastic → kinetic → heat/sound correctly.
